newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Tobacco industry in talks with attorneys general.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Tobacco industry in talks with attorneys general.

text.p: By Gail Appleson, Legal Correspondent
U.S. Tobacco executives are negotiating for the first time with state attorneys general on a possible settlement of massive litigation against the industry, several attorneys general said Wednesday.

They said the first round of talks, which began about two weeks ago, ended Wednesday in Virginia. Steve Berman, a Seattle lawyer involved in negotiations, said no date for the next set of talks had been scheduled.

"We are at beginning stage ... this is first time I've ever seen a tobacco representative sitting across the (negotiating) table in the three years that we've been involved in the litigation. This is really significant," Minnesota Attorney General Hubert Humphrey told Reuters in a telephone interview.
"The fact these talks are going on is a real reflection that these tobacco companies know they are on the ropes," he said.

Humphrey added that he did not feel any of the proposals made so far are adequate and Massachusetts Attorney General Scott Harshbarger, who is also involved in the talks, warned that a settlement is "not imminent."
Berman said, however, that a great deal of progress had been made at the talks and he thought it was a possible that a final deal could be reached this year.

Philip Morris Cos. Inc. Chairman Geoffrey Bible and RJR Nabisco Corp. Chairman Steven Goldstone attended the beginning of talks and other tobacco executives remain at the bargaining table, Berman said.
Humphrey and Harshbarger are among the 22 attorneys general who have sued the industry to recoup Medicaid costs of smokers.

News about the settlement talks pushed tobacco stocks up sharply. Philip Morris rose $4.375 to to close at $43.25, RJR Nabisco rose $3.25 to close at $33.50 and Loews Corp., which owns Lorillard Tobacco Co., rose $5.375 to close at $91.75, all on the New York Stock Exchange.
Pressure has been steadily building on the tobacco industry to seek a resolution to mounting lawsuits and other legal developments against it.

Last month the smallest of the major cigarette makers, Liggett Group, owned by Bennett LeBow's Brooke Group Ltd., reached a historic settlement with the attorneys general. Under terms of the accord, it became the first tobacco company to admit that nicotine is addictive and it also agreed to turn over internal documents that could prove damaging to the entire industry.

The timing of the Liggett accord could not have been worse for the industry. The first Medicaid case, which was filed by Mississippi, is scheduled to go to trial in July. Other state Medicaid trials are expected to begin this year, as well as a major second-hand smoke class action suit brought on behalf of airline flight attendants.
Even this week, the plaintiffs lawyer who last summer won a verdict against Brown & Williamson Tobacco Corp., a unit of Britain's B.A.T Industries, is trying a case against Reynolds.
The Justice Department also is conducting a criminal investigation of the industry concerning allegations that it withheld health information from government agencies.

One source close to the talks between the attorneys general and tobacco representatives said the parties had discussed the establishment of a $300 billion fund to pay for smoking-related injuries over a 25-year period, but Humphrey would not comment on the figure.

He said that any settlement would have to meet certain requirements, including that the industry changes the way it does business, stops marketing to minors and pays an amount that could cover the treatment of smoking-related illnesses.
"The attorneys general are not focused on just the money ... we are focused on the overall change and reform of this industry," Humphrey said.
Mississippi Attorney General Mike Moore, a lead negotiator, issued a statement through his office confirming that negotiations had intensified recently.

"Our main concern is the children and we are working with the public health community to make sure that issue is taken care of first and all other issues come after that," Moore said in his statement.

In Washington, the White House said it was monitoring the talks but stressed that it was not a direct participant. "We are closely monitoring the negotiations," White House Press Secretary Mike McCurry said.

Anti-tobacco forces said the amount of money being discussed is far less important than the fact that the sessions mark the first time that tobacco representatives and high-ranking industry officials have directly discussed a settlement with the plaintiffs' side.

"It's impressive that we have the industry on the run," said Richard Daynard, chairman of the Tobacco Products Liablity Project at Northeastern Law School. However, he added that the $300 billion figure does not begin to cover the costs of smoking-related illnesses.
"It's a nice start. It's real interesting that the companies are finally coming to the table but it's a long way to final settlement," Daynard said.
Three senators who have actively pushed for controls on tobacco said they were highly sceptical of the negotiations.
Sens. Frank Lautenberg of New Jersey, Richard Durbin of Illinois and Ron Wyden of Oregon, all Democrats, said they expressed their reservations in a letter to President Clinton.
